message.content:
Based on the search results, here is a comprehensive guide to what medicine you should take when you get a cold:

## Important First Points

- **There is no cure for the common cold** — it is caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not work against colds
- Most colds get better on their own within **7 to 10 days**
- The goal of medication is to **relieve symptoms** while your body fights the virus

## Over-the-Counter Medicines for Symptom Relief

### 1. Pain Relievers / Fever Reducers
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** — for headaches, sore throat, aches, and fever
- **Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin)** — for pain and fever reduction
- **Important:** Do not take multiple medicines containing the same ingredient, as this can lead to accidental overdose

### 2. Decongestants
- Help with **stuffy nose** and sinus pressure
- Available as tablets (e.g., Sudafed with pseudoephedrine) or nasal sprays (e.g., Afrin, Neo-Synephrine)
- **Warning:** Nasal sprays should **not be used for more than 3 days** in a row due to "rebound congestion"
- Not recommended for **children under 6 years old**

### 3. Antihistamines
- May help with **runny nose and sneezing**
- Some cause drowsiness (e.g., Benadryl with diphenhydramine)
- Research shows they are **not very effective** for cold symptoms specifically

### 4. Cough Medicines / Syrups
- Evidence suggests they don't work much better than a placebo for colds
- **Honey** can relieve cough for adults and children **over 1 year old**
- Not typically recommended for young children

## Non-Medicine Remedies That Help

- **Rest** — plenty of sleep helps your body recover
- **Fluids** — drink lots of water, warm teas, or broths
- **Humidifier or steam** — helps ease congestion
- **Saline nasal spray or rinse** — clears mucus without rebound effects
- **Gargling salt water** — soothes sore throat
- **Hot lemon and honey drink** — soothes throat (not for children under 1 year)

## Important Warnings

| Group | Precautions |
|-------|-------------|
| **Children under 6** | Avoid most OTC cough/cold medicines; use only children's acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever |
| **Children under 4** | Do NOT use antihistamine or decongestant cold medicines |
| **High blood pressure** | Avoid decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine) — they raise blood pressure; look for decongestant-free options like Coricidin HBP |
| **Pregnant women** | Consult a pharmacist or doctor before taking any medicine |
| **Everyone** | Never give aspirin to children or teenagers |

## When to See a Doctor

- Fever lasting more than 3-4 days
- Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement
- Trouble breathing or chest pain
- Severe headache or symptoms that worsen after improving
- You have chronic conditions (diabetes, heart/lung/kidney disease) or weakened immune system

## Bottom Line

Choose medicines based on your **specific symptoms**:
- **Fever/aches** → Acetaminophen or ibuprofen
- **Stuffy nose** → Decongestant (short-term only)
- **Runny nose/sneezing** → Antihistamine (limited effectiveness)
- **Cough** → Honey (for adults/children over 1)

Always read labels carefully, avoid doubling up on the same active ingredient, and consult a pharmacist if you're unsure which medicine is right for you.

---

1. https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/common-cold/
2. https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html
3. https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20351611
4. https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/decongestants-antihistamines-cold
5. https://www.webmd.com/cold-and-flu/cold-medicine-treatment-when-what-how
6. https://www.cdc.gov/antibiotic-use/media/pdfs/Common-Cold-508.pdf
